1057-poems-with-the-ballad-of-reading-ga:
Oscar Wilde's poems gather here beside his last great work, "The Ballad of Reading Gaol," written after his release from prison. The early lyrics praise beauty, Rome, and art, while the Ballad tells of a fellow prisoner hanged for murder and of the pity Wilde learned inside.

The contrast gives the book its force: the young aesthete's lush verse against the older man's stark lines on shame and mercy. "Each man kills the thing he loves" runs through the Ballad like a bell. The volume stands as Wilde's poetic testament, and it moves readers still.
19944-the-yotsuya-kwaidan-or-o-iwa-inari:
The Yotsuya Kwaidan is Japan's most famous ghost story, retold here from the Tokugawa era. This edition's maps follow the Edo Sunago of 1866. District details come from an Edo map published in 1857. The Go Edo Zusetsu Shuran supplies further topography. Such care grounds a ghost tale in real streets. Oiwa, the wronged wife, haunts those streets forever in Japanese tradition.

James de Benneville retold Tokugawa tales for English readers. The kwaidan, or weird tale, was his specialty. Oiwa's story mixes murder, betrayal, and relentless haunting. It still anchors Japanese horror today. The maps show Edo as the tale's first audience knew it. This volume is folklore and city history together.
20144-the-fourth-book-of-virgil-s-aeneid:
Virgil's Aeneid, book four, tells of Dido and Aeneas in Carthage. This volume pairs it with book nine of another famed classical work. The pages discuss the stuff from which such poems were built. Critics, it notes, were not always fair in judging the results.

Book four of the Aeneid holds one of the great love tragedies in verse. Dido's passion and death have moved readers for two thousand years. School and college readers long met Virgil in volumes like this one. Readers get Latin epic with the aids and notes students once used daily.
20390-elements-of-structural-and-systema:
Douglas Houghton Campbell wrote Elements of Structural and Systematic Botany as a textbook for high school and college courses. It teaches both how plants are built and how they are sorted into groups. Clear terms and steady order guide the student through each topic.

Campbell adds only as much classification as will make the links between plant groups clear. He explains the rules on which the sorting rests. The aim is practical. Students should be able to recognize the commoner types of the different groups, in the field or the laboratory.
20661-the-romance-of-an-old-fool:
The Romance of an Old Fool, published in 1902, is a novel told through the diary of its elderly hero. From childhood he has kept a diary, a running comment on the daily incidents of his pleasant but uneventful life. Into that quiet record, love arrives absurdly late.

He confesses his small revenges in its pages. When Bunsey's society seemed too assertive and familiar, he punished the offender by retreating to his diary. The old fool's romance is watched by the whole town, and by himself, with a mix of shame and delight. The book treats late love gently and comically.
20730-for-the-sake-of-the-school:
Angela Brazil helped shape the classic British school story, and For the Sake of the School opens in a rush of travel. A porter shouts for girls to stand back on a crowded platform. Pupils bound for Glanafon and Graigwen swarm with boxes, talk, and nerves at the start of term.

School loyalty gives the book its title and its core test. Brazil's girls face scrapes, strains in friendship, and calls to put the school first. Her tales made boarding-school life vivid for generations of young readers. This one keeps her usual mix of fun, feeling, and firm school spirit.
20734-roman-antiquities-and-ancient-myth:
Roman Antiquities and Ancient Mythology was made for classical schools, to teach the daily world behind Latin texts. The preface notes fresh changes, with some parts cut so the book kept its size. Questions were dropped to make room for new matter.

Inside, pupils found Roman customs, offices, dress, houses, and gods set out in clear order. Such manuals once stood on every Latin student's desk. They turned dry grammar work into a picture of real life in Rome. This volume shows how schools in that era taught the ancient world as a full way of life, not just a language.
20750-journal-of-the-proceedings-of-the-:
Crustacean shells open the third zoology volume of the Linnean Society's journal proceedings. Spence Bate argues that shell structure can settle doubtful species. He applies the point to the genus Galathea and names a new species there.

Learned papers like this one built Victorian natural science piece by piece. Each claim rests on close looking at real specimens. The Linnean Society, named for the great classifier Linnaeus, spread such work worldwide. Modern readers can watch taxonomy grow in real time, one crab shell and one careful note at a time, across these dense pages.
21034-the-corner-house-girls-at-school:
Dot, the youngest Corner House girl, knows Allie Neuman of Willow Street well, she ventures. Grace Brooks Hill sends the sisters back to school in this 1915 tale. Allie will share Dot's grade at school, past Mrs. Adams's house on the way.

Ruth, Agnes, Tess, and Dot fill the Corner House set with sisterly life. School terms, new friends, scrapes, and home joys drive this volume's plot. Hill writes warm tales of girls who work, play, and stick fast together. This school entry shows the sisters beyond their famous house, in classrooms where their bond meets fresh tests.
21083-transactions-of-the-american-socie:
Paper No. Paper No. 1154 in the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers reports on the Bergen Hill tunnels. They formed part of the Pennsylvania Railroad's New York Tunnel Extension. Engineer F. Lavis presented it in April 1910. The tunnels form the section west of the Hudson River, known as Section K.

Bergen Hill is a hard trap-rock ridge, the lower end of the Hudson Palisades. Lavis describes two parallel single-track tunnels driven through it, on a line near 32nd Street in New York. Plates, figures, grades, and rock conditions fill the paper. It records how American rail engineers pushed a main line under a river and hill.
21324-recollections-of-old-liverpool:
A nonagenarian who was born in Liverpool and remembered into his nineties published these recollections in 1863, with a view of the city in 1813. His chapters roam widely. They cover the ducking stool and the Flashes in Marybone, the launch of ships, the inside of a slave ship, and the town's privateers. The salt trade gets pages of its own.

John Howard the prison reformer, the Borough Gaol, fairs, footpads, and country walks to Everton all appear. Later chapters turn to elections, with George Canning and Henry Brougham stirring divisions. Few books preserve a port city's everyday past so personally, from a man who watched Liverpool grow across two centuries.
21656-the-princess-of-the-school:
Angela Brazil opens The Princess of the School with a Christmas rush dodged, in a tale copyrighted in 1920. Miss Walters packs her pupils off by the first trains to beat the crowds. The girls themselves raise no objection to the early start.

Chapters promise a stolen joy-ride, a Valentine party, and a girl disinherited. Princess Carmel arrives as the new owner's kin, and a secret society forms. Sicily, the Casa Bianca, and the high seas widen the tale beyond the school. Frank Wiles draws the pictures. Brazil, queen of the school story, mixes lessons, larks, and loyalty in her known bright style.
21847-dr-wortle-s-school:
A school scandal tests a proud headmaster in Anthony Trollope's Dr. Wortle's School, published in two volumes in 1881. Dr. Jeffrey Wortle, rector of Bowick and master of its school, was esteemed by others and by himself. He had taught at Eton for ten years before taking the living. Into his ordered world comes a new usher, Mr. Peacocke, and with him a mystery.

The doctor asks his question, and the story is told: a secret in the usher's past that polite society cannot forgive. The bishop, the Stantiloup family, and Lord Carstairs all take their parts. Trollope treats the matter with his usual fairness, letting every side speak. It is one of his shorter, sharper novels of character under pressure.
21955-the-secret-wireless-or-the-spy-hun:
Boy wireless operators hunt German spies in Lewis E. Theiss's The Secret Wireless, published in 1918 while the Great War still raged. Henry Harper sits in the doorway of his father's backyard workshop, where the Camp Brady Wireless Club has its headquarters, reading the morning paper. Suddenly he springs up, fist clenched. His idea sets the patrol preparing for action.

A message in cipher, a pursuit in the dark, and a clue from the air fill the chapters. Theiss dedicated the book to a Bucknell professor of electrics who helped him keep the wireless work true. The boys change ciphers, race too late, and at last capture the spies. It is wartime adventure for the first radio generation, patriotic and proud of its sparks.
21993-the-devil-s-pool:
French peasant love is told with a poet's care in George Sand's The Devil's Pool. Jane Minot Sedgwick and Ellery Sedgwick Englished it in 1894. Sand opens with Holbein's plowman, urged on by a skeleton with a whip through stony soil. Then her own tale softens the picture: Germain, a skilled husbandman and widower, is sent to find a new wife. He travels with little Marie and his small son Petit-Pierre across the heath.

The devil's pool of the title waits in the woods where the travelers lose their way at night. An appendix describes a country wedding in full, favors, feast, and cabbage rite. Sand loved the Berry countryside and its people. This short novel is her tenderest portrait of them.
22101-wood-folk-at-school:
William J. Long, a minister and naturalist, wrote the Wood Folk books to teach children about animals. In Wood Folk at School he takes readers into a deep hollow in the big woods. A fallen tree bridges the stream, and Long sits on the mossy trunk to watch. Bridges, he says, are for crossing, so every neighbour must pass his seat.

Foxes, deer, birds, and small beasts come by, each with lessons to learn. Long treats the woods as a school where the young are trained by their parents. His stories blend sharp watching with kindly invention. Critics of his day argued over how much he made up, but young readers loved the wood folk then and the books stayed in print.
22113-peggy-stewart-at-school:
Gabrielle E. Jackson's Peggy Stewart at School, published in 1918, belongs to her Peggy Stewart series for girls. Peggy, the daughter of a naval officer, goes away to boarding school. The book opens in fierce August heat at home, with dry grass and dust over everything. Indoors, all is cool and inviting by contrast, but school waits.

At school Peggy meets new girls, new rules, and the small politics of dormitory life. Jackson writes about lessons, friendships, scrapes, and homesickness. Her heroine is lively, loyal, and quick to take the lead. Such girls' school stories were a thriving kind in 1918, and Peggy Stewart was among their popular heroines.
22208-cruel-barbara-allen-from-coals-of-:
Cruel Barbara Allen takes its title from the old ballad of the hard-hearted Barbara. David Christie Murray's tale, from his Coals of Fire set, opens on a man remarkable for nothing but dreamy eyes. Those eyes could flash with inward lightnings at times. His hair was lank, his figure thin and ungraceful, and his clothes sat awkwardly on him.

Neighbours thought him sulky, and some found his voice bumptious. Murray builds the story on the gap between that outside and the life within. The ballad's theme, love scorned until too late, hangs over the plot. It is a moody piece, showing Murray's interest in misjudged, solitary men.
22250-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science was a Philadelphia monthly that mixed fiction with fact. This volume gathers issues from the 1870s, when the magazine was in its prime. One travel piece describes a city ringed by the Atlas mountains, extremely picturesque. Steamers stay only a few hours at each port, the writer laments, leaving scarcely time to enjoy the views.

Serial novels, poems, science notes, and essays share the volume's thick pages. Lippincott's later became famous for printing The Picture of Dorian Gray entire in one issue. The bound volumes show the respectable middle of American magazine culture: improving, various, and built to be kept.
22601-hiawatha-and-the-iroquois-confeder:
Horatio Hale wrote Hiawatha and the Iroquois Confederation, a study in anthropology about the founding legend of the Five Nations. The catalog record gives no year. Hale, a linguist and ethnologist, treated Native traditions as serious historical evidence at a time when many scholars did not.

The sample weighs deep questions about the antiquity of human types, arguing that people appeared on earth with much the same body and mind they keep today. Around such arguments, Hale examines the Hiawatha story and the league it credits him with founding. The book stands as an early, respectful attempt to read Iroquois tradition as history. It still rewards readers interested in the roots of anthropology and in the confederation itself.
22609-the-writings-of-james-russell-lowe:
James Russell Lowell's Political Essays form one volume of his collected writings in prose and poetry. The catalog record gives no year. Lowell, poet, editor, and diplomat, was among the most feared political pens of nineteenth-century America, and this volume gathers his essays on public men and public questions.

The sample shows his manner at full stretch. A ruler, pressed by the needs of his position, slides by degrees into crime and luxury. Those were the very sins that once horrified him in his hermitage days. Lowell's prose mixes learning, wit, and moral judgment in long, rolling sentences. These essays let modern readers watch a leading American man of letters judge the politics of his age, from slavery to Reconstruction and beyond.
22995-miss-pat-at-school:
Pemberton Ginther's Miss Pat at School, published in 1915, opens on a confession. Her friend confesses that her calm face is a fraud. Inside, she admits, she is more stirred up than ever before in her life. The feeling runs too deep for words, and none will come.

Miss Pat belongs to the era's boarding-school series for girls, where new terms bring new rivals, secrets, and loyalties. Ginther keeps the excitement in the emotional register her excerpt shows, feelings too deep for words at the school gate. Lessons, pranks, and friendships fill the chapters between. The book preserves the hopes such fiction sold its readers, that school would test them gently and friendship would see them through.
23240-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-no-:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 336, for October 1843, is an issue of the famous monthly review. Its critics could be severe about heavy books. One review in this issue grants that a work is abstract, calls for unbroken attention, and offers little in the way of lighter or amusing matter.

Yet the same review praises searching thought and clear views, aptly expressed. That balance was Blackwood's trademark: sharp judgement in lively prose. Readers get a sample of Victorian reviewing at full strength, where a dull subject could still earn respect if the thinking was strong and the writing lucid.
301-the-ballad-of-reading-gaol:
Oscar Wilde, himself a prisoner at Reading, wrote of a trooper hanged for killing the woman he loved. The Ballad of Reading Gaol, dedicated to C. T. W., opens with a man in shabby grey who looks wistfully at the sky. Wilde walked another ring of pain beside him.

Two versions appear here, both tracking the condemned man's last days, the trial men, and the prison routine. Wilde turns pity for one killer into protest against all hanging. The ballad's refrain on each man killing the thing he loves became famous. It stands as Wilde's last great poem.
3123-the-novel-and-the-common-school:
Warner writes here about American health, manners, and school reading within two generations. The physical state of the people has improved greatly, he says, more in the West than in the East, but markedly everywhere. A foreign traveler once blamed a dry, stirring climate and a feverish hunger for quick change for a decline in the race. That traveler would now find little to support his theory.

The essay links that bodily improvement to the common school and its books. Novels, Warner argues, belong in the education of ordinary readers, not kept from them. Well chosen fiction can train taste and morals for pupils who will never reach a college, and the school that scorns it wastes a plain tool for good.
3842-memoirs-of-jean-franc-ois-paul-de-g:
Cardinal de Retz begins his memoirs with his birth and family, setting the stage for a life spent at the center of French trouble. The preface lists his titles, second Archbishop of Paris, Abbot of Saint Denis, and sovereign of Commercy. It traces his line from Albert de Gondi, duke and marshal, through his father Philippe Emanuel, general of the galleys. Retz was born at Montmirail in October 1614, into a house built for power.

The first book then follows his youth and entry into the church and the state, with Paris already stirring. A later passage shows a cardinal hurrying a count into civil war by chicanery, while the Duke of Bouillon presses for war whatever the cost. Readers who start here will meet Retz before the Fronde made him famous, ambitious, learned, and already dangerous.
3843-memoirs-of-jean-franc-ois-paul-de-g:
Cardinal de Retz opens his second book with a maxim for ambitious men, that they should begin public life with some notable act to strike the people's imagination. He recalls preaching on All Saints' Day before a crowd glad to see an archbishop in the pulpit. Then he faced an archbishopric sunk in temporals and spirituals by his uncle's sordidness and neglect. Retz owns frankly that his own corrupt inclinations would bear down honor and conscience.

The book then moves into the Fronde, as Paris example governs Guienne and Provence and everything shakes and totters. The queen shares the people's hatred with Cardinal Mazarin, while the Duke of Orleans shares their contempt with his favorite. Readers who like memoirs without varnish will find Retz a candid and cunning guide to civil war.
3844-memoirs-of-jean-franc-ois-paul-de-g:
Cardinal de Retz devotes his third book to the struggle between Mazarin and the Prince de Conde, who had saved the cardinal from the gallows. Mazarin, seeking to shed his debt, courts the house of Vendome, old opponents of Conde, while Paris fills with libels and ballads against the cardinal. Retz admits it suited his party to let attacks on Mazarin run, though attacks on the queen had to be stopped.

A grim scene follows, as two men condemned for libeling the queen cry from the scaffold that they die for verses against Mazarin, and the crowd rescues them from justice. Retz also confesses how fear of failure made him first refuse a cardinal's hat, then chase it with headlong haste. The book shows conspiracy from inside, told by a conspirator who admires his own craft.
3845-memoirs-of-jean-franc-ois-paul-de-g:
Cardinal de Retz covers the crisis of Mazarin's return in his fourth and fifth books. In December 1651 Parliament resolves to send deputies to the king, to forbid all governors to give the cardinal passage, and to warn foreign princes why he was removed. When a voice proposes setting a price on Mazarin's head, Retz and the other spiritual councillors retire, since canon law bars clergy from votes on life and death.

The narrative then follows the Duke of Orleans to Limours, where panic seizes him so hard that he takes musket fire for rejoicing as soldiers come to invest his palace. Messengers bring word that all is quiet, but he trusts no one and watches the window for drums. The books show a revolution eating its own leaders, with Retz at the center of the fear.
3884-memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoi:
Madame Campan, first lady in waiting to Marie Antoinette, opens her memoirs with a warning about Louis the Sixteenth. The king kept a crowd of confidants, advisers, and guides, chosen even from factions that attacked him, yet never fully disclosed himself to any one of them. He held the reins of secret intrigues in his own hand, and from that secrecy came the want of cooperation and weakness conspicuous in his measures.

The preface promises that chasms will appear in any detailed history of the Revolution for that reason, and Campan fills them from the queen's rooms. A Marly drawing room scene, where Lauzun teases a marshal about snuff taken with a chairman, shows her eye for rank and ridicule. Readers who like the queen's side of the story will find a loyal and observant witness.
3885-memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoi:
Madame Campan begins her memoirs at fifteen, when she was appointed reader to the king's daughters. She describes a court where Queen Maria Leczinska has just died, the dauphin died three years earlier, the Jesuits are suppressed, and Choiseul rules. Etiquette survives in all its Louis the Fourteenth forms, but dignity alone is wanting, and gaiety has fled to Paris, since the king thinks of nothing but the chase.

A duel pardon shows the young dauphiness at work. A grieving mother supplicates royal children for an hour and wins the culprit's life. A rival lady then sneers that even du Barry was solicited. Campan records the malice without comment. Readers who like Versailles before Marie Antoinette will find a sharp-eyed girl learning the court.
3886-memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoi:
Madame Campan's third volume follows Louis the Sixteenth in his first months, dwelling at La Muette, Marly, and Compiegne before settling at Versailles. The young king examines his grandfather's papers and promises the queen to share anything on the man in the iron mask, whose fame a celebrated writer's pen had fed. After research and talk with Maurepas, he reports no secret paper explains the prisoner, a dangerous intriguer and subject of Mantua, enticed to the frontier and held first at Pignerol.

Court life fills the rest, as young coxcombs imagine the queen notices them from her incognito theatre box, and Lamballe hands ushers the list of persons admitted to the queen's closet. Campan writes with a lady in waiting's precision. Readers who like Versailles before the storm will find a calm and detailed book.
3887-memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoi:
Madame Campan's fourth volume tours the royal visitors who came to Versailles in the last century's close. Northern sovereigns take a fancy for travel. The Grand Duke of Russia, later Paul the First, arrives with his wife as the Comte and Comtesse du Nord, presented on May 20, 1782. The queen receives them with grace, though nervous, and Louis speaks to Paul with more confidence than he showed Joseph the Second.

The comtesse, tall and stiff with German learning, fares less well at first. A lighter passage has the queen charging Campan to warn her when flowers cease to become her, and Campan refusing with a Gil Blas joke about the Archbishop of Granada. A jeweller's gathering diamonds hints at a darker story ahead. Readers who like court visits will find ceremony and wit in equal share.
3888-memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoi:
Madame Campan's fifth volume, the second book of her Revolution narrative, opens with the Tennis Court oath and the royal sitting of June 23. The king declares the orders must vote separately and threatens to act himself for the people's good. The queen counts Necker's absence as treachery, since he had promised to accompany the king and then disavowed the step. Insurrections on July 11, 12, and 14 open the disastrous drama, with the Bastille taken and Flesselles and Launay massacred.

The royal visit to Paris follows. The king speaks with firm grace of his pleasure among his good city's people, and the queen loudly corrects Bailly when he drops the word confidence from the speech. The Tuileries, unready and long given to courtiers, receives the family in haste. Readers who like the Revolution day by day will find Campan at her most urgent.
3889-memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoi:
Madame Campan's sixth volume covers the spring of 1791, when the royal family tries to leave Paris and cannot. The king, tired of the Tuileries, orders dinner at Saint Cloud, but guards mutiny at one o'clock, shut the gates, and refuse passage. Two men near the carriage are ill treated, Campan's father-in-law loses his sword, and the family returns indoors, seeing in the outrage a justification for escape in the people's eyes.

The queen has prepared since March, giving Campan secret orders for linen and gowns that Campan calls useless and dangerous. A tender scene follows, as the king taps at Campan's door to comfort her against injustice and calumny, noting that the royal family suffers the same. Readers who like the flight to Varennes from inside will find a book of plans, fear, and loyalty.
3890-memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoi:
Madame Campan's seventh volume follows the queen from the Tuileries to the Temple and toward the scaffold. Robbed of her purse on the way to the Feuillans, the queen borrows twenty five louis from Campan's sister. That loan later serves as pretense to arrest both women and leads to the sister's death. Campan herself, refused at the Feuillans gates on August 11 and again on the 12th despite tears and a deputy's intercession, cannot join her mistress.

The Temple chapters show drums beating, sections arming, and a rumored rescue by four or five hundred devoted men. Santerre arrives at eight in the morning, the king rises, and Clery carries his last farewell to his wife. Readers who like testimony at its gravest will find a book of loyalty, loss, and the Revolution's final cruelty.
4299-the-whirlpool:
George Gissing opened this novel with Harvey Rolfe dining with care at his London club. Rolfe knows good food without quite mastering it, and he enjoys the comfort his money now buys. He has known poverty, and London landladies' tables, and he values his present ease all the more.

The whirlpool of the title is London society itself, with its money, marriages, and restless talk. Gissing follows Rolfe and his circle through drawing rooms and clubs, tracing how ambition and affection pull people under. It is a large, patient novel of late Victorian London life.
4940-grace-harlowe-s-senior-year-at-high:
Grace Harlowe's senior year at high school begins on a sunny October afternoon at Oakdale station, where Grace and her chums Anne, Nora, and Jessica say goodbye to Hippy, Reddy, and David. The boys leave for a four-year course at an eastern college, and the girls face a school year without them.

The novel follows Grace through her final year: friendships, school rivalries, and the small puzzles of growing up, including a puzzling resemblance that opens the story. The catalog record leaves the author unnamed. Readers get a warm school story from the series tradition, centered on loyalty among friends rather than on a single crisis.
5141-what-katy-did-at-school:
Susan Coolidge's school story sends Katy Carr away to boarding school after the events of the earlier book. It follows her first year among new friends, teachers, and rules. Chapters take Katy from a country excursion called Conic Section through the autumn term, a secret society for the suppression of unladylike conduct, and the long wait for spring.

Coolidge writes warmly about friendship, mischief, unfair blame, and growing up, with letters and Christmas boxes marking the school year. The book remains a favourite of classic girls' fiction, and it offers a gentle, detailed picture of nineteenth-century school life as Katy learns to balance spirit with self-control.
5602-the-boy-scouts-patrol:
Ralph Victor wrote The Boy Scouts Patrol, illustrated by Rudolf Mencl, as a boys' adventure about a patrol finding its feet. Chapters run from A Monkey Trick and Finding Money through Up the River, The Enemy Makes a Raid, and The Colonel, to Forming the Patrol, Organized, A Challenge, and A Defiance. Pepper takes a message, Pepper goes missing, and the message itself becomes a quest.

The story follows lads of about sixteen through river trips, raids, pursuits, and a judge's office, ending in a race and a conclusion. Victor writes outdoor adventure with teamwork at its center. Young readers get a lively early scouting tale, full of pranks, pursuit, and patrol spirit.
5760-two-trips-to-gorilla-land-and-the-c:
Richard Burton recounts his first volume of travels in Gorilla Land, published in London in 1876. Chapters land at the Rio Gaboon, depart through a tornado, survey the geography of the Gaboon, and meet minor tribes and the Mpongwe people. Later chapters visit Sanga-Tanga, village life in Pongo land, the river journey upward, a specimen day with the Fan people, and Mr, Mrs, and Master Gorilla.

Burton writes as an explorer and observer, mixing geography, language notes, and firsthand encounters with humor and bluntness. Modern readers should note that his language about African peoples reflects Victorian attitudes and needs critical reading. As a travel record, the volume preserves a vivid, detailed picture of the Gaboon region before later colonial change.
5761-two-trips-to-gorilla-land-and-the-c:
Richard Burton's second volume of Two Trips turns from the Gaboon to the Congo, published in London in 1876. Chapters sail from Fernando Po to Loango Bay. They visit Sao Paulo de Loanda and celebrate a festival with a trip to Calumbo. Cruising along shore, they enter the Congo River and pass factories and a slave depot. Boma outfits the party for the interior, and the march leads through Banza Nokki toward the Yellala cataracts.

Burton records river navigation, trade posts, and peoples met along the way with an explorer's detail and a Victorian traveler's bluntness. Modern readers should read his descriptions of African peoples critically, as products of their era. As a record of the Congo before later upheaval, the volume offers geography, incident, and a hard-won route toward the cataracts.
6063-the-bobbsey-twins-at-school:
Laura Lee Hope sends the Bobbsey twins to school, opening on a circus train where Nan asks how much longer they must ride. Bert offers to sit by the window and watch telegraph poles and trees go by, and their father smiles, seeing Bert has two thoughts for himself and one for Nan.

Chapters follow Snoop gone, a queer dog, Snap doing tricks, Danny Rugg mean, a scare, a children's party, Thanksgiving, first snow, a night alarm, and a confession. The fat lady's letter and Snap and Snoop close the book. School days bring tricks, questions, and small mysteries for the twins.
6416-entertainments-for-home-church-and-:
Frederica Seeger, edited by Theodore Waters, offers entertainments for home, church, and school in a practical handbook. Household games open the book, with Going Shopping, Hit or Miss, a game of rhymes, and a most improbable story. Animated art, guessing character, and tongue twisters follow, with French rhymes, Ant and Cricket, and a spoonful of fun.

Church and school socials bring charades, including Cicero, Attenuate, and charades on the Grecian islands. Optical illusions, table games for adults, outdoor games, and holiday games complete the set. A note on staging adds that a royal crown need only be golden on the side toward spectators, and cotton velvet reads as silk through gauze. Seeger writes for hosts who want fun without fuss.
6575-the-purple-parasol:
George Barr McCutcheon opens with young Rossiter on a fast train north, hating the task his firm has set him. He must watch a young, lovely wife of seventy-year-old Wharton, and the job feels like police work, not law. Rossiter grumbles that he never wanted to be a cop, and that Wharton got just what he might have expected.

From that sour start grows a tale of love, age, money, and a parasol that marks its heroine. McCutcheon writes with wit and a light touch, letting Rossiter's gruff voice carry the comedy. The Purple Parasol is a smart, old-style romance of a man who takes a shabby job and finds his heart in it.
721-the-birds-christmas-carol:
Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote this Christmas tale about Carol Bird, a frail child known as a little snow-bird, who longs to give joy to others. Though she is often confined to her room, she plans a Christmas carol party for the poor Ruggles children next door, with food, gifts, and song. Her family helps her carry out the plan.

The tale is tender without being mawkish, and it turns on Carol's wish to share what little strength she has. Wiggin writes the children's world with warmth and humour. The book has lasted as a gentle holiday story about giving, kindness, and the light one small life can cast.
7235-the-bride-of-fort-edward-founded-on:
Delia Bacon's Bride of Fort Edward grows from an incident of the Revolution, yet Bacon warns readers at once that it is not a play. She chose dialogue in scenes arranged for the reader alone, wholly unadapted to the stage. That form best suited her purpose: presenting anew the passions and events of a day long buried in the past.

The preface guards against misconception with care, insisting that the work be judged as reading, not as theatre. Its scenes let voices from the Revolution speak in their own heat, while the author shapes the whole for private reflection. Bacon's little book thus joins history to drama without ever asking for footlights.
7283-short-stories-and-selections-for-us:
Emilie Kip Baker compiled and annotated these short stories and selections for secondary schools, with questions for study. Her table runs from Louise de la Ramee's Leaf in the Storm and Maurice Hewlett's Cats through Balzac, Axel Munthe, and Richard Jefferies. Herman Melville's Taboo, George Sand's school days at the convent, and Louisa Alcott in Brittany complete the set.

Each piece comes with notes and questions, so that pupils can read a story and then think hard about it. Baker mixes famous names with lesser-known work, favouring tales that teach by feeling as much as by craft. The volume serves as a classroom reader with a critic's guidance built in.
737-the-bobbsey-twins-at-school:
Laura Lee Hope took the Bobbsey twins, Bert, Nan, Freddie, and Flossie, back to school for a new term of lessons and play. Class work, games, and small rivalries fill their days, while pets and friends add comic trouble. The twins learn to help classmates, own up to faults, and keep their spirits up when plans go wrong.

The tale is gentle and orderly, with each chapter bringing a fresh schoolroom scrape or kindness. Hope writes for young readers in plain, cheerful prose, and the twins' good humour carries the book. It stands as a classic school story of its era, valued for its warmth and its simple lessons in fair play.
911-tales-of-the-fish-patrol:
Jack London wrote these tales of the Fish Patrol on San Francisco Bay, a water so large that storms often hide its far shore. The patrolmen chase oyster pirates, smugglers, and poachers, in boats that race the tide and the law. White and Yellow, the opening tale, sets the scene of bay, fog, and hard men.

London draws on his own youth on the bay, and his stories carry the salt, danger, and humour of that life. The patrol tales praise courage and fair play, while showing the rough code of watermen. The book is a lively set of sea adventures, and a fine introduction to London's California years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce:
Bristol takes its origin as a diocese from measures aimed against the Church. Its Catholic history is very brief, with only one bishop acknowledged by the Holy See. It was one of six bishoprics Henry VIII tried to found by Act of Parliament in 1542. He built them out of the spoils of suppressed monasteries, beside Oxford, Westminster, Gloucester, Peterborough, and Chester.

The city, then a leading town and chief seaport, was chosen for the new see. Its Augustinian abbey church was saved from demolition by the king's order after the house was plundered in 1539. That house had been founded by Robert Fitzharding in 1133. At the dissolution the dedication changed from Saint Augustine to the Holy Trinity, and the arms of the see show three ducal crowns in gold on black.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faldstool:
A faldstool is a movable folding chair used by bishops at pontifical functions. When no throne stands in the church, the bishop sits on it. It is covered in cloth of red, green, or violet, matching the liturgical colour. The name comes from the folding stool it stands on.

Rich examples include a gold and jewelled chair given to Clement IV. Hugh Pudsey, bishop of Durham, owned a silver faldstool in the twelfth century. The article notes where the chair stands during Mass and processions. It also lists the ministers who carry and set it in place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liverpool:
Liverpool is one of the thirteen dioceses Pius IX set up for Catholic England in 1850, when he restored the hierarchy. It covers North Lancashire, western South Lancashire, and the Isle of Man, with Salford taking the eastern half of the south.

By 1910 the diocese counted about 366,611 Catholics, 184 churches and chapels, and 458 priests, plus some seventy convents holding a thousand nuns. Schools taught 74,100 children, and homes cared for the blind, the aged poor, orphans, and fallen women. Town tables show Liverpool itself with 143,000 Catholics, then Preston, St. Helens, Wigan, and the rest in turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-protocol:
Protocol, in this short encyclopedia entry, is a notary's word with three linked senses. First, it means the opening formula of a public deed. That formula names the reign, the time and the place. Second, it means the bound register where a notary enters each deed in date order. Third, it means the first draft itself, written small and kept by the notary. From that draft a larger fair copy is made for the parties.

Courts whose registrars still carry the name of notary keep the same usage for their own registers. Because public deeds must be trustworthy, only originals or certified copies count as proof. A copy gains its standing when the notary witnesses on its face that it matches the original. That guarantee goes by the Latin name fides instrumentorum, trust in documents. The entry cites Justinian's Novels and the 1910 rules of the Rota.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-joseph-:
Joseph Oriol, called the wonder-worker of Barcelona, was born there on 23 November 1650 and died there on 23 March 1702. He studied at the University of Barcelona and took his doctorate in theology in 1674. Ordained priest in 1676, he won a benefice in the church of Our Lady of the Pine after a visit to Rome in 1686.

His priestly life stood out for penance, deep humility, and wise guidance of souls. Longing for martyrdom, he set out for Rome in April 1698 to offer himself for the foreign missions, but fell sick at Marseilles and returned home. People who were dying, blind, deaf and dumb, lame, or paralysed were said to be cured by him at once. Pius VII beatified him in 1806, and Pius X canonized him in 1909.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-anchor-as:
Hope, pictured as an anchor, is the theme of this short entry on early Christian symbols. In the ancient world the anchor already stood for safety at sea, since ships depended on it in storms. Christians took up the familiar emblem and gave it a deeper sense: trust in salvation to come, not merely rescue in this life.

Hebrews chapter 6 supplies the key text, calling hope an anchor of the soul, sure and firm. Peter, Paul, and early Fathers use the same image, and the entry traces it through catacomb inscriptions and carvings, including a fragment from the cemetery of Saint Domitilla. For readers of early art, it explains why an anchor carved beside a name spoke of faith beyond death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tiraspol:
The Diocese of Tiraspol, in southern Russia, was one of the largest dioceses in the world, covering 462,504 square miles. Suffragan to Mohilev, it took in Saratov, Samara, Kherson, Ekaterinoslav, Taurida and Bessarabia. It held 350,000 Latin Christians, mostly descendants of German colonists in a hundred parishes, with 40,000 Armenian Catholics in fifty parishes and a small Chaldean community.

About 210 priests served the diocese, and the bishop lived at Saratov, where seminaries for priests and boys trained new clergy. Religious orders were not permitted. German colonists had settled the empty southern lands at Catherine II's invitation in the later eighteenth century, keeping their German village names. Bishop Franz Xaver Zottmann, appointed in the nineteenth century, built its cathedral and seminaries and made it one of Russia's best organized dioceses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zahle-and-for:
Zahle and Forzol is the Greco-Melchite diocese whose wandering title tells a story of mistaken geography. In the seventeenth century, Antioch's patriarch moved the diocese of Seleucia Pieria to Maaloula in Lebanon for safety. The reason was later forgotten, a phantom town of Seleucia Libani was invented and matched to Maaloula, though no such town ever stood. When the see moved from Maaloula to Forzol, the Seleucia title travelled with it, already borne by a Forzol bishop in 1760.

Since 1849 the bishop bears the titles of Zahle, Forzol, and Beqaa, residing at Zahle since 1768. Zahle itself dates only from the late seventeenth century, when Catholics fled there in crowds under Lebanon's emirs. Now about twenty thousand strong, nearly all Catholics, the town saw Druses destroy two thousand houses in 1860 and massacre Christians. The diocese counts thirty thousand Catholics, forty-seven priests, and thirty-three churches.

The wind operators get their upgrade. The turbine was GE 1.5 ESS. The development was controller. The operators got upgrades.

The study was system. The data were nuclear. The 1998-2024 were cooling. The RCIC were study. The isolation were core.

doe-osti-3374720-loss-of-flow-conditions: SFR got flow-loss-designed, and this DOE text covers pool-type in-pile. The pages detail the loss findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The conditions were modern. The data were nuclear. The SFR were design. The in-pile were experiment.
doe-osti-3377657-engaging-with-utilities: Utilities got stakeholder-engaged, and this DOE slides cover key engagement. The pages detail the engaging findings. The energy folks get their deck. The format was slides. The deck was energy. The stakeholders were key. The engagement were utilities. The energy were deck.
doe-osti-3388186-navigating-the-complian: EPAct got tool-navigated, and this DOE guide covers reporting tools. The pages detail the navigating findings. The transport folks get their data. The program was alternative provider. The data were transport. The guide were user. The EPAct were reporting.
doe-osti-3683723-compositional-homogenei: 316L got homogeneity-compositioned, and this DOE text covers rapidly solidified steel. The pages detail the compositional findings. The materials folks get their data. The fusion was laser powder-bed. The data were material. The 316L were steel. The solidified were rapidly.
entertainments-for-home-church-and-schoo:
Entertainments for Home, Church and School, by Frederica Seeger and edited by Theodore Waters, is a handbook of games and socials. Six opening chapters cover household amusements. Going Shopping, Hit or Miss, tongue twisters, and the Tailless Donkey fill the first lists. Church and school socials take four chapters next. Optical illusions, table games for adults, and outdoor games follow.

Holiday amusements, pastimes for children, singing games, and games of arithmetic round out the twenty chapters. Every entry is a recipe: players, props, and rules in order. Before radio, such books were a community's entertainment department. A hostess or a teacher with Seeger's volume could fill an evening in any hall in America. The games themselves are period pieces now. Cushion dances and lemon pigs survive chiefly here, between the rules for shadow buff and the Knight of the Whistle.
govdocs-archive_org-narcissus-and-goldmu:
Hermann Hesse, the German novelist and Nobel laureate, wrote Narcissus and Goldmund in 1930 and set it in medieval Germany. Its two heroes are opposites bound in friendship: Narcissus, a monk and thinker, and Goldmund, a wanderer ruled by the senses.

Goldmund leaves the monastery for a life of love, art, and wandering, while Narcissus stays on the path of the spirit, and the novel moves between their two ways of being. Late in life the friends meet again and reckon with what each path cost. It is Hesse's most beloved tale of the divided self.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIControl_FBI_: Andy Purdy wrote a memorandum on August 17, 1977 about a search for missing autopsy materials. Purdy was working in the period when a House committee was again investigating the assassinations of the 1960s. The surviving record gives the author, date, and subject but not the memo's findings, so it stands as a dated staff note on the hunt for missing medical evidence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIDomesticInte:
Joseph McLellan wrote about the FBI's files on Bertolt Brecht, the German playwright who lived in American exile. Working from declassified records, the article shows the Bureau watching a writer. On May 16, 1943, J. Edgar Hoover himself authorized microphone surveillance aimed at Ruth Berlau, Brecht's close collaborator, in Santa Monica.

A playwright under a microphone is a measure of wartime domestic intelligence. The files treat theater people as security subjects and record their private talk. McLellan's article lets readers see that surveillance through the documents the government later released, files the Bureau once kept closed.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GaleWilliamCol_:
FBI agents interviewed George Saudikas Jr. of Sparks, Nevada on November 9, 1963. The subject was his association with a Los Angeles church organization, the First Church of Christ, Christian, which he had joined through his cousin. The interview took place thirteen days before President Kennedy was assassinated.

Thousands of such interviews filled the Bureau's files, each fixing one person's ties and movements. A church connection in Los Angeles, reached through family, was enough to earn a Nevada man a recorded conversation. The report preserves that small act of checking, from the last calm weeks before Dallas.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-UnionCollegeSch: nsia-UnionCollegeSchenectadyNY Union College Schenectady NY: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files.
govdocs-archive_org-the-criminal-history: Karlheinz Deschner spent his career writing a criminal history of Christianity, and volume 9 reaches the New World. It covers genocide in the Americas through the early modern era. Deschner, a German historian, builds his indictment from records of conquest, forced conversion, and church power. Supporters call the series fearless; critics call it one-sided. Either way, the ninth volume presses its case on the bloodiest ground in the story.
grace-harlowe-s-senior-year-at-high-scho:
Jessie Graham Flower's Grace Harlowe's Senior Year at High School closes her Oakdale school series. The title page prints Flower's name as author of the earlier Plebe, Sophomore, and Junior volumes. Grace and her chums Anne, Nora, and Jessica stand on the station platform in October. The boys are leaving for college, and senior year begins without them.

A puzzling resemblance opens the mysteries: a new girl who looks like Grace. Fire alarms, a Thanksgiving bazaar, and a thief in the night fill the school year. The Phi Sigma Taus, the girls' society, meet with a loss and a confession. A haunted house and the message of the violin carry the spring. The parting of the ways ends the book, as graduation scatters the class. Flower writes wholesome school fiction of friendship tested and kept.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
The December 1880 Lippincott's, Volume Sixteen, opens in Colorado. An historical Rocky-Mountain outpost anchors the first article. June-like sunshine warms a snow-covered mountain landscape there. Pueblo today thrives as an aggressive pioneer city, the writer says.

Legend claims Coronado stopped his northward march on that spot. There he supposedly founded New Spain's farthermost outpost. Three hundred forty years separate legend from the modern town. The article promises contrasts greater than earth and sky provide. Fontaine qui Bouille's leafless cottonwoods fringe the sombre plains. The average traveller journeys westward from the Missouri past it.
margaret-smith-s-journal-and-tales-and-s:
Margaret Smith's Journal fills volume five of John Greenleaf Whittier's works. An editor's note of 1866 warns of small inaccuracies in the record. Allowances must be made for the prejudices of its period. Yet the journal gives a lifelike picture of the colonial past.

Margaret Smith writes from the hearths of seventeenth-century New England. Secretary Rawson and his family figure large in her pages. Whittier fashioned the journal from history, legend, and imagination. Tales and sketches of old New England follow it here. The volume shows the Quaker poet as a storyteller of the past. His love for colonial homes and ways fills every page.
memoirs-of-jean-franc-ois-paul-de-gondi-:
Book two of Cardinal de Retz's memoirs opens with a bold maxim. Jean Francois Paul de Gondi wrote the memoirs himself. They treat great events in the youth of Louis XIV, under Mazarin.

Men who serve the state, he says, should start with a striking act. He preached first on All Saints' Day to make his mark. Then he weighs his uncle's weak rule of the archbishopric. He admits his own bent to sin, yet vows to do his office well. He gave the right hand to guests and saw them to their coach. Such care built the name he needed for his plots.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoinette:
Volume one of Campan's memoirs of Marie Antoinette opens with her preface. Jeanne Louise Henriette Campan served as first lady in waiting. Her tale was called the historic memoirs of the Queen's court.

Louis XVI chose guides even from the factions that attacked him. Sincerity, she says, he showed to very few of them. His want of joint action made his measures weak in the end. She points readers to other memoirs for the reign of Louis XV. Weak joint action is her core charge against his rule. That charge sets the frame for the queen's tale to come.
nasa-tm-19660028393-analysis-of-condensi:
Donald R. Packe, Andrew A. Schoenberg, Kent S. Jefferies, and Roy C. Tew wrote this report at NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland. It concerns SNAP-8, a nuclear power system designed to make electricity in space. The authors focus on one control problem inside its heat-rejection loop: the pressure where vapor condenses back to liquid.

They used a steady-state computer simulation of the loop and condenser. With it, they studied how outside disturbances and worn parts change the condensing pressure. The study found that control may be needed to keep pressure within safe limits for the turbine and pump. Of the methods tried, condenser coolant bypass flow control looked most promising.
nasa-tm-19700016328-experimental-effects:
Robert J. Simoneau and Kenneth J. Baumeister of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 cryogenic engineering meeting. It reports tests of film boiling on thin wires in liquid nitrogen. In film boiling, a vapor layer wraps the hot wire and slows heat flow.

The team took data and high-speed films during the tests. They used two wire sizes, one very thin and one thicker. Runs covered a range of pressures and degrees of subcooling. Subcooling means the liquid sits below its boiling point. The results show how pressure, subcooling, and wire size each change the boiling behavior.
nasa-tm-19700026614-doppler-observable-m:
Howard G. de Vezin of the Mathematical Physics Branch wrote this internal note on February 16, 1968. It was issued by the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston. It models the Doppler readings used by the Apollo real-time orbit determination program, the system that fixed a spacecraft's path from ground tracking.

The note studies current ways of computing the Doppler observable, then presents a range-difference technique. That technique gets the integrated Doppler count straight from the change in signal path length across the counting interval. Near Earth and the Moon it holds clear advantages over the older expansion method, with no truncation error. Its shorter, simpler form won it the place in the Apollo program.
poems-with-the-ballad-of-reading-gaol:
Oscar Wilde's Poems appear in this twelfth Methuen edition of 1913, edited after his death by his friend Robert Ross. A note by Ross explains the contents: Wilde's 1881 volume of poems entire, the Sphinx of 1894, Ravenna of 1878. The Ballad of Reading Gaol of 1898, plus two poems, Désespoir and Pan, printed for the first time from manuscript Ross had lately discovered. A few uncollected pieces from the 1908 uniform edition are omitted.

The arc inside one cover is startling: the jeweled, aesthetic lyrics of a young Oxford dandy give way to the Sphinx's riddling splendor. Then to the Ballad, written from the ruin of Wilde's imprisonment, where every man kills the thing he loves. Ross's careful editing, with publication details for each poem, made this the standard Wilde for a generation of readers.
practice-book-leland-powers-school:
Leland Powers issued this Practice Book for his school of oratory in 1909, gathering the selections his students declaimed. His acknowledgments map the territory: Daniel Webster's discourse on eloquence from Little, Brown; Charlotte Perkins Gilman's poem A Conservative. Extracts from John Ruskin; poems by Richard Burton; and, by arrangement with Houghton, Mifflin, pieces by Edward Rowland Sill and Ralph Waldo Emerson. Lewis B. Monroe's Sixth Reader supplied the vocal exercises.

The index is a recitation-hall canon: Tennyson's Brook and Coming of Arthur, Browning's Cavalier Tunes, Joaquin Miller's Columbus, Burton's Across the Fields to Anne, and Emerson's Each and All. Powers trained speakers in the elocutionary tradition, where voice was character and a poem well delivered was an education. The book preserves both a curriculum and a taste: what Boston in 1909 thought a young person should be able to say aloud, beautifully, from memory.
rod-of-the-lone-patrol:
H. A. Cody, author of The Long Patrol and The Frontiersman, wrote this boys' tale for McClelland and Stewart of Toronto, under a copyright of 1916. He dedicates it to his three little boys, Douglas, Kenneth, and Norman, who are anxious to become Boy Scouts. A line from Longfellow heads the book: a boy's will is the wind's will.

A Waif of the Night opens the contents, and Giving and Receiving and The Widow's Visit follow. Rodney develops, Captain Josh takes a hand, and chums come to the rescue in the middle chapters. His First Good Turn and Scout Work name the Boy Scout thread plainly, in a story of a lone patrol learning its trade.
samuel-f-b-morse-his-letters-and-journal: Samuel F. B. Morse: His Letters and Journals, in two volumes, is shown here at Volume II, issued in November 1914. The work was edited and supplemented by his son, Edward Lind Morse. It is illustrated with reproductions of Morse's paintings and with notes and diagrams bearing on the invention of the telegraph. A portrait of Morse faces the title page, and a quotation from Milton on the invention all admired heads the volume. The contents open at Chapter XXI, covering October 1, 1832 to February 28, 1833.
short-stories-and-selections-for-use-in-:
Emilie Kip Baker compiled this school reader of tales and chosen pieces, with notes and study questions. Walter Scott's library at Abbotsford serves as the front picture. A leaf in a storm by Louise de la Ramee leads the contents, followed by Maurice Hewlett on cats.

Balzac, Melville's Typee, George Sand's convent school days, and Louisa Alcott in Brittany all appear. John Burroughs writes on the Adirondacks, while Lady Brassey climbs Kilauea. Teachers get a wide, well-chosen set that mixes tale, travel, and nature writing for young readers in secondary school.
songs-of-the-springtides-and-birthday-od: Algernon Charles Swinburne wrote Songs of the Springtides. A Birthday Ode stands with the songs. Both come from Volume III of his Collected Poetical Works. William Heinemann printed the London issue in 1917. A first printing by Chatto came in 1904. The opening pages list all six volumes of the set. Poems and Ballads stands first among them. Tristram of Lyonesse and Atalanta in Calydon appear in Volume IV. Studies in song and roundels fill Volume V.
stories-from-the-italian-poets-with-live:
Leigh Hunt's Stories from the Italian Poets, With Lives of the Writers, appeared in two volumes in MDCCCXLVI, or 1846. This second volume treats Boiardo and Ariosto, giving for each a notice on his life and genius before the tales begin.

For Boiardo, Hunt retells Angelica's adventures, the death of Agrican, and the Saracen friends, with a piece called Seeing and Believing. For Ariosto he follows Angelica and her suitors, Angelica and Medoro, and the jealousy of Orlando, then adds Astolfo's journey to the moon and the tale of Ariodante and Ginevra. Romance, magic, and knightly love fill the retellings.
tales-of-the-fish-patrol:
Jack London's Tales of the Fish Patrol appeared in a London printing from William Heinemann in 1914. The tales draw on London's own youth as a sailor on San Francisco Bay, where state patrol boats fought men who broke fish laws.

White and Yellow, the first tale, says the broad bay can prove more harsh to ships than the open sea. It tells how Chinese shrimp crews used fine bag-nets that killed vast numbers of young fish. Readers get brisk sea tales of risk, law, and hard men, where a patrolman's life and a poacher's catch both hang on tide and nerve.
the-ballad-of-reading-gaol:
Oscar Wilde wrote his ballad in memory of C. T. W., once a trooper of the Royal Horse Guards, who died at Reading Prison in Berkshire on July 7, 1896. Two versions of the poem are listed in the contents. The opening stanzas describe a condemned man in shabby grey.

He did not wear his scarlet coat, the poem says, because blood and wine are red and both were on his hands. He walks among trial men, looking wistfully at the small blue sky prisoners see. A voice whispers that the fellow is to swing, turning a single hanging into a picture of prison dread.
the-birds-christmas-carol:
Kate Douglas Wiggin dedicated her Christmas tale to three children, Bertha, Lucy, and Horatio. Contents use bird images throughout: a little snow-bird, drooping wings, a bird's nest, and birds taught to fly. A closing chapter is called The Birdling Flies Away.

Chapter one opens very early on Christmas morning, with soft snow falling, as a child is born in the Bird household. The family had meant to name a girl Lucy, but a Christmas baby needs special thought. Mr Bird leaves naming to his wife, Donald proposes Maud after a schoolmate, Paul proposes Luella after his nurse, and Uncle Jack favours the mother's name.
the-bobbsey-twins-at-school:
Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins at School for young readers. Its parts run from a circus train, a lost cat, and a queer dog to school days with a mean boy named Danny Rugg. Thanksgiving, the first snow, a night alarm, and a charge of smoking all come up. The book ends with a fat lady's note and the pets Snap and Snoop.

The tale opens on a train, where Nan Bobbsey asks her mother how much more of the ride is left. Her twin Bert says he will take the seat by the glass if she is tired. He adds that the poles and trees flying past may be what tires her. Their father smiles, since Bert has thought twice of his own wish and once of his twin.
the-boy-scouts-of-the-eagle-patrol:
Lieut. Howard Payson wrote The Boy Scouts of the Eagle Patrol. Its chapters run from scouts on the trail and a cruise to an island to a rescue and a bully's trick. Stolen uniforms, a lost hydroplane found in a queer way, a contest won, and camp life fill the mid heads. Late heads bring peril, a storm, a missing boy, and a rescue by smoke Morse.

The tale opens near Hampton, on the south shore of Long Island. Scrub oak and pine part, and a lithe boy of about seventeen steps into a small clearing. He wears a neat brown khaki suit, canvas leggings, and a soft campaign hat turned up at one side. On the hat sits a metal badge shaped like the three-pointed arrow head used on old maps to mark north. Below it a scroll bears the scout words: Be Prepared.
the-boy-scouts-patrol: Ralph Victor wrote The Boy Scouts Patrol, with art by Rudolf Mencl. The chapter list starts with A Monkey Trick and Finding Money. Two and Two, Up the River, and Out of the River come next. The Enemy Makes a Raid and The Pursuit follow. Looking for a Clue leads to Forming the Patrol. A Challenge and A Defiance follow. Pepper Takes a Message and Where Was Pepper raise a scare in the late heads. The Message, In the Judge's Office, and A Narrow Escape close the list shown.
the-bride-of-fort-edward-founded-on-an-i:
Delia Bacon wrote The Bride of Fort Edward, founded on an incident of the Revolution. In a preface from New York, dated July 7, 1839, she is firm on one point: the work is not a play. It was not meant for the stage and could not be put on one. She chose the form of dialogue to lay out the passions and events of a day long buried in the past, in scenes shaped for the reader.

The tale, Bacon says, is tied to a well-known crisis in the nation's past, and is itself part of the record of those days. Yet she asks to be read for a deeper truth. Her theme is a law of the mind and its unseen guard, seen in the seeming sacrifice of one life in the great moves made for the race.
the-devil-s-pool:
George Sand's The Devil's Pool appears in a subscribers' edition printed at Philadelphia by George Barrie and Sons under a 1901 copyright, completely translated by George B. Ives, with etchings and drawings by Edmond Rudaux. A picture caption shows little Marie watching her three sheep on the common land.

In an opening notice Sand says she began the tale as the first of a series of rustic pictures, to be gathered as The Hemp-Beater's Tales. She had no theory and no aim to work a revolution in literature. The romance of rustic manners, she notes. It has lived in all ages and forms, pompous, affected, or artless. The dream of country life has always been the ideal of cities and of courts. In following that dream, she insists, she has done nothing new.
the-life-of-thomas-lord-cochrane-tenth-e:
Thomas, eleventh Earl of Dundonald, joined with H. R. Fox Bourne to complete the life of his father, Thomas Lord Cochrane, in a volume published in 1869. A preface says the book resumes where Cochrane own Autobiography of a Seaman stopped at his death. The son hoped to finish sooner and explains the delay.

Cochrane papers sat with a helper who died before using them, and strangers held them for years. Cost and trouble attended their recovery. Volume one now tells a daring naval captain public life, from frigate fame through disgrace, foreign service, and return.
the-lives-of-the-poets-of-great-britain-: Volume III of The Lives of the Poets of Great Britain and Ireland, dated 1753, was compiled by Mr. Cibber and other hands from materials in many books and from the manuscript notes of the late Mr. Coxeter. Only the title page and the volume's contents list are present here, so the lives themselves do not appear. The list names eighteen poets, among them Denham, Aphra Behn, Etherege, Shadwell, Dryden, Sedley, Sackville, Earl of Dorset, Farquhar, Ravenscroft, and John Philips.
the-luckiest-girl-in-the-school: Angela Brazil wrote The Luckiest Girl in the School, copyrighted in 1916 by Frederick A. Stokes Company and published in the United States in 1922 by A. L. Burt Company, with illustrations by Balliol Salmon. Only the title page and part of the contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The chapters shown are A Great Change, An Entrance Examination, Seaton High School, The Symposium, and Aunt Harriet. An illustration caption quotes a girl faltering, "Those aren't my papers," suggesting a schoolgirl mix-up early in the book.
the-manor-school: L. T. Meade's The Manor School is dated 1903 in its heading and was published by the Mershon Company under a 1903 copyright. Front matter alone is present: a title page and the start of the contents, with none of the story itself. The contents shown open with chapter one, The Attic of Desire, at page one, and chapter two, The Mystery, before the list breaks off. Meade is identified as the author of A Bunch of Cherries, Daddy's Girl, The Time of Roses, and Bad Little Hannah.
the-novel-and-the-common-school:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote an essay on reading, schools, and the health of American life. He begins with the body rather than books. Americans, he says, have grown stronger and better looking in two generations, thanks above all to more food, better cooked and more varied than any people had known before.

Warner then turns to the mind. Reading is more widespread, schools reach nearly everyone, and books and papers multiply. His question is whether mental growth has kept pace with physical growth, and what part the novel should play in common schools. The essay links diet, schooling, and taste into one picture of national progress.
the-prose-works-of-william-wordsworth-fo: Alexander B. Grosart collected The Prose Works of William Wordsworth for the first time, with additions from unpublished manuscripts, in three volumes published in 1876. Volume I is labelled Political and Ethical. Grosart, asked by the holders of Wordsworth's manuscripts, dedicates the set to the Queen. He explains that a recovered transcript of a poem from a gift copy sent to Windsor suggested her as dedicatee. The pages at hand break off inside that dedication; none of Wordsworth's prose is shown.
the-purple-parasol:
George Barr McCutcheon sends young lawyer Sam Rossiter north on the Empire State Express with a job he dislikes. Rossiter works for the New York firm of Grover and Dickhut and has been asked to watch the young wife of elderly millionaire Godfrey Wharton.

Mrs. Wharton, twenty-five to her husband's seventy, has fallen for actor Everett Havens, and gossip has spread through fashionable society. Rossiter calls the assignment police work and a Peeping Tom job, yet his ambition keeps him on the train. The setup promises a reluctant detective story about marriage, reputation, and class in New York.
the-rebel-of-the-school: Mrs. L. T. Meade's school story is presented by its Chicago publisher, M. A. Donohue and Company, alongside a long list of her other girls' books, including school favorites, tomboy tales, and stories of girls in ten thousand and the true blue. Here only the title page and the publisher's series list are present, so the rebellion itself does not appear.
the-reconstructed-school:
Francis B. Pearson, Ohio's superintendent of public instruction, sets out a program for schools in a World Book Company volume of 1921. Chapter one surveys the task before the school, arguing that people who come to think alike tend to act alike, as long-married couples show in shared action.

Chapters then relate past and future to the present and take up virtues one by one, including integrity, appreciation, aspiration, initiative, imagination, reverence, responsibility, loyalty, democracy, and serenity. Pearson treats schooling as character formation for a democracy. Educators will recognize debates about purpose that still continue.
the-seven-great-monarchies-of-the-ancien: George Rawlinson, Camden Professor of Ancient History at Oxford, wrote The Seven Great Monarchies of the Ancient Eastern World. The work appeared in three volumes, with maps and illustrations. This record holds volume one. Its subtitle promises the history, geography, and antiquities of seven empires. The pages shown give the title and the contents of volume one only. The first monarchy, Chaldaea, opens the list. Its chapters treat the country, climate, people, and language. No chapter text follows.
the-vitalized-school: Francis B. Pearson, superintendent of public instruction of Ohio, wrote The Vitalized School for the Macmillan Company. Copyright was taken in 1917 and the book reprinted in January 1918. Pearson also wrote The Evolution of the Teacher and Reveries of a Schoolmaster. The material present here is the title page and a full contents list, so the educational argument does not appear. Seventeen chapters move from the teacher and the child toward democracy and patriotism. Later headings treat complete living, the artist teacher, and agriculture.
the-whirlpool:
George Gissing opens The Whirlpool at a London club dinner with Harvey Rolfe, an imperfect epicure. Rolfe selects dishes thoughtfully and peers at his wine like a connoisseur, though he knows only Bordeaux from Burgundy and his club has no culinary fame. He is conscious of his shortcomings and never vaunts his satisfactions, having known poverty and London landladies' tables.

Few club members truly like Rolfe, and his place there came through Hugh Carnaby, a rambler and sportsman now married into Mrs. Ascott Larkfield's family. Rolfe studied medicine, quit in disgust, entered business, and withdrew on inheriting a competency. Gissing gives him no purpose beyond enjoying himself, much reading, and an indolent, inconsistent conservatism.
the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first-colle: Volume two of Walter Scott's 1808 collected Works of John Dryden is shown through its contents and an opening advertisement. Plays listed include The Wild Gallant and The Rival Ladies. The Indian Queen and The Indian Emperor follow. Secret Love, or the Maiden Queen, also appears. The advertisement concerns Congreve's earlier edition of Dryden's dramatic works. The plays themselves start past the pages given here.
three-expeditions-into-the-interior-of-e:
Major T. L. Mitchell, surveyor-general, wrote journals of three expeditions into eastern Australia, and this record presents volume one of a carefully revised second edition. T. and W. Boone published it at London. Mitchell describes Australia Felix and the colony of New South Wales.

His preface admits the journals were written after laborious days that exhausted mind and body. He asks readers to excuse defects while hoping for interest. Australia, he says, lacks classical associations but offers a vast, mysterious country and singular productions. Readers get exploration writing from Britain's growing Australian colonies.
transactions-of-the-american-society-of-:
Paper No. 1156 in the Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers covers the western half of the Pennsylvania Railroad terminal site in Manhattan. B. F. Cresson Jr. describes a work area of about 6.3 acres between Ninth and Tenth Avenues. The site takes in parts of 31st and 32nd Streets.

Ninety-four buildings stood on the land, mostly homes and church property, and all had to come down first. The railroad bought most plots outright, though some needed condemnation. One church gained a new site on 34th Street, with rebuilt church, rectory, convent, and school. Contractors demolished the buildings between April and August 1906 and kept the salvaged materials.
two-trips-to-gorilla-land-and-the-catara:
Richard F. Burton's Two Trips to Gorilla Land and the Cataracts of the Congo appeared at London in 1876, in two volumes. Volume one opens with a dedication letter dated at Trieste on January 31, 1875, addressed to a Sir George whose own exploring ran to the Arctic. Burton contrasts their lots in the letter.

The north took his friend, while Burton's lot fell in Sind, Arabia, Africa, and Brazil. A true traveller, he writes, enjoys most the adventures most unlike his own. He calls the book a plain, unvarnished tale of a soldier-traveller. Latin verses and a Byron jab about Timbuctoo travels head the title page.
what-katy-did-at-school:
Susan Coolidge continued Katy Carr's story in What Katy Did at School. The book opens just after the visit that ended the first Katy book. Elsie and John take a famed trip to a place they call Conic Section. The family teases them about it for a long time after.

The contents promise a new year and a new plan, a stay the girls call the nunnery, and a club known by initials. Later chapters bring wrongs, change, letters, and Christmas boxes. Katy faces school rules, friends, and tests of her temper. Readers who loved the home tale can watch Katy grow in a stricter world.
